concepts.title: Affinity-Based Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Affinity-based segmentation groups items by modeling a distance metric that measures the similarity between patterns or the likelihood they belong to the same object.
concepts.content:
Affinity-based segmentation is based on the idea of affinity, where a distance metric is modeled to determine whether two items should be grouped. This metric usually measures how similar two patterns are or how likely they are to be part of the same object. For example, a simple affinity function over pixel pairs could be the Euclidean distance between their color values. Pixels with high affinity should belong to the same group, while pixels with low affinity should belong to different groups.

Methods using this principle include graph cuts, spectral clustering, and Markov random field (MRF)-based clustering. A modern approach involves contrastive learning, which is a natural fit because it learns from similarities (positive pairs) and differences (negative pairs). Contrastive methods learn an embedding where datapoints with high affinity are nearby and those with low affinity are far apart. Once this embedding is established, clustering can be performed using an algorithm like $k$-means.

While color distance can serve as an affinity, the method becomes more interesting with nontrivial affinities, such as those derived from human judgments or self-supervised measures. Self-supervised contrastive learning methods like SimCLR, MoCo, and DINO train mappings from image patches to embedding vectors. By running these methods densely across an image, a feature map is created where each pixel's value is an embedding vector similar to other pixels likely to appear in the same scene. Applying $k$-means to this feature map results in effective segmentation.

(see figure: Image segmentation using $k$-means over DINO @caron2021emerging features)
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional clustering often struggles with complex visual structures. Affinity-based segmentation solves this by defining a similarity metric (affinity) between elements. This allows the system to group pixels or regions based on learned relationships rather than just raw pixel values, making it possible to capture semantic or perceptual coherence in an image.
concepts.recap_md: - Affinity measures the similarity or likelihood that two items belong to the same group.

concepts.title: Edge Detection
concepts.one_liner: Edge detection aims to represent image content through sparse, stable boundaries that often correspond to scene geometry like depth discontinuities.
concepts.content: Edge detection is a complementary problem to segmentation, as an image partition can be represented either by segment assignments or by the boundaries between them. Early vision algorithms focused on edge detection under the premise that edges form a compact representation of image content. Edges are relatively sparse and remain stable despite nuisances like noise and lighting. Furthermore, specific edge structures relate to scene geometry; for instance, an edge representing an occluding contour indicates a depth discontinuity at that location in the scene.
concepts.motivation_md: Edges provide a sparse and robust representation of an image, filtering out noise and lighting variations while preserving essential structural information like object boundaries and depth changes.
concepts.recap_md: - Edges provide a compact, sparse representation of an image that is stable against noise.

concepts.title: Line Drawings
concepts.one_liner: Line drawings represent the edge structure of an image in a way that is highly intuitive to humans, though their utility for machine vision remains an active area of research.
concepts.content: Line drawings are a method of representing the edge structure in an image. Their high interest to humans suggests that representing images via edge structure may be fundamentally useful. While there is active research in computer graphics regarding the modeling of line drawings, it remains unclear if this representation will eventually prove as compelling for visually intelligent machines as it is for humans.
concepts.motivation_md: Humans can easily recognize objects from simple lines, suggesting that edge-based representations contain the most critical information for visual understanding.

concepts.title: Layer-Based Representations
concepts.one_liner: Layer-based representations capture depth by modeling a scene as a stack of planes, approximating 3D structure through parallax.
concepts.content:
Layer-based representations capture aspects of depth by modeling a scene as a stack of planes, similar to the multiplane camera used in early animation. In this approach, different elements of a scene—such as the sky, mountains, and foreground characters—are drawn on separate glass planes. Shifting these planes creates parallax, where foreground layers move faster than background layers. This serves as a rough approximation of the 3D world and is often referred to as a 2.5D representation, providing a way to handle depth without the computational expense of full 3D modeling.

concepts.motivation_md: Modeling the full 3D geometry of a scene is computationally expensive. Layer-based representations provide a simpler alternative that still captures essential depth cues like occlusion and parallax.
concepts.recap_md: - Scenes are modeled as a stack of planes to approximate 3D depth.

concepts.title: 2.5D Representations
concepts.one_liner: 2.5D representations are pseudo-3D models, such as layers, that capture depth aspects without the full expense of 3D modeling.
concepts.content: In computer vision, layer-based representations are popular for capturing aspects of depth without the expense of modeling a fully 3D world. These layers and other related pseudo-3D representations are sometimes called 2.5D representations.
concepts.motivation_md: 2.5D representations bridge the gap between flat 2D images and complex 3D models, allowing systems to reason about depth and layering efficiently.
concepts.recap_md: - 2.5D representations are pseudo-3D models that capture depth via layers.

concepts.title: Ordinal Structure
concepts.one_liner: Ordinal structure refers to the relative depth ordering of objects, such as which item is on top of another.
concepts.content: Layers in a representation capture ordinal structure, which describes the relative ordering of objects rather than their exact position in metric space. This is often the primary structure of interest in tasks where relative depth is key; for example, determining which piece of paper is on top of a pile.
concepts.motivation_md: In many practical tasks, knowing the exact distance to an object is less important than knowing its relative order (e.g., what is in front of what).
concepts.recap_md: - Ordinal structure captures the relative depth ordering of objects.

concepts.title: Emergent Groups
concepts.one_liner: In modern neural networks, structures like objects and contours are emergent properties of hidden layers rather than explicit human-designed components.
concepts.content: While traditional methods like edge detection and bottom-up segmentation are less common in modern vision systems, perceptual organization remains present. In these systems, structures such as objects, contours, and layers are emergent in the hidden layers of neural networks rather than being explicitly designed by humans. For instance, object detectors have been observed to emerge within neural networks trained for tasks like colorization.
concepts.motivation_md: Modern deep learning suggests that explicit manual definitions of visual parts are not always necessary, as networks naturally learn to organize visual information to solve complex tasks.
concepts.recap_md: - Perceptual structures like objects and contours emerge naturally in the hidden layers of deep networks.

concepts.title: Why Group?
concepts.one_liner: Grouping is a form of representation learning that discovers language-like structures, such as objects and relationships, from unsupervised principles.
concepts.content:
Grouping is a special case of representation learning, serving as a substrate for downstream analysis and processing. Perceptual organization involves structures like objects, spatial relationships, shapes, and events. While current trends in computer vision map images to text to use natural language processing tools, perceptual organization aims to achieve similarly powerful representations through bottom-up grouping rules rather than human-language supervision. It is about discovering language-like structures from unsupervised principles to understand what constitutes an "object." Perceptual groups can also extend beyond the limits of language, representing coherent structures in our minds that may not have specific names.

(see figure: How many objects do you see?)
concepts.motivation_md: To interact with the world, we need to move beyond raw pixels to meaningful entities. Grouping provides the necessary structure for reasoning, planning, and high-level understanding.
concepts.recap_md: - Grouping provides a foundation for downstream tasks like object recognition.

concepts.title: Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Segmentation is the problem of partitioning an image into regions that represent different coherent entities.
concepts.content:
**Segmentation** is the problem of partitioning an image into regions that represent different coherent entities. There is no single definition of what constitutes a coherent entity, as it varies by task; a segment might be a nameable object, a region of a single material, or a physically distinct piece of geometry.

(see figure: There are multiple ways you might segment any given image, and each way will highlight different world properties. This cactus branch could be viewed as (a) a single segment (the "branch"), (b) two...)

Segmentation can be framed as a clustering problem where each pixel is assigned to one of $k$ clusters. Two common approaches to this problem include assigning similar pixels to the same cluster or assigning pixels to the same cluster if there is no boundary between them.
concepts.motivation_md: Segmentation is a fundamental step in computer vision that allows machines to isolate individual objects or regions from a complex scene for further analysis.

concepts.title: K-Means Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: K-means segmentation clusters pixels based on feature similarity, such as color, to partition an image into regions of constant appearance.
concepts.content:
$K$-means is a simple clustering algorithm that can be applied to segmentation by treating each pixel as a datapoint. The simplest approach uses the pixel's color as its feature vector. For example, using $ab$ color values allows an image to be visualized as a scatter plot of color distributions.

(see figure: Different regions of coherent color in the image correspond to clusters in the scatter plot of all the $ab$-values of the image's pixels. In general, segmentation can be reduced to the problem of...)

$K$-means finds clusters in this color space and segments the image by assigning each pixel to the cluster of its color value. Each pixel in a cluster can then be colored by the mean color of that cluster.

(see figure: $K$-means segmentation on the fruits example.)

This method effectively finds segments with roughly constant color. While it can succeed on images where objects are defined by color similarity (like a zebra against a background), it fails on complex patterns not defined by color similarity.

(see figure: (top row): $k$-means segmentation succeeds on a seemingly hard image. *Photo source*: Fredo Durand. (bottom row): $k$-means fails on an image that, to our eye, looks no more complex.)
concepts.motivation_md: K-means provides a computationally efficient way to perform basic segmentation by assuming that objects are composed of pixels with similar visual features like color.

prereq.rationale: K-means segmentation is a specific technique used to solve the broader problem of image segmentation.
Affinity-based segmentation is a major paradigm for solving the image segmentation problem by modeling pairwise relationships.
Ordinal structure is the specific type of information (relative depth) that layer-based representations are designed to capture.
Line drawings are defined as a specific method for representing the edge structure extracted from an image.

overlay.rationale: K-means serves as a concrete demonstration of how clustering can be used to partition an image into regions of constant appearance.
Affinity-based methods are contrasted with simpler clustering like K-means, focusing on distance metrics and likelihood of object membership rather than just feature similarity.
Both concepts deal with representing depth and layering in a way that is intermediate between 2D and 3D metric space.
Modern systems rely on emergent structures in hidden layers rather than explicit, hand-designed components like traditional edge detectors.
Layers, which capture ordinal structure, are one of the specific types of organization that emerge in modern vision systems.
Edge detection and segmentation are described as dual, complementary approaches to the problem of partitioning an image into segments or boundaries.
The text identifies layer-based models as a specific and popular instance of the broader category of 2.5D representations.
